summary: On October 15, 2023, city officials announced a three-year project to make the subway, bus, and tram systems more accessible to people with disabilities, the elderly, and others with mobility challenges. The plan combines rapid repairs, long-term infrastructure renovations, tech tools, staff training, and public engagement, and is estimated to cost $500 million. It would be funded through bonds, federal grants, a slight fare increase, and private partnerships, with the DoT promising progress reports and annual independent audits.
one_line: The city announced a three-year, $500 million plan to make subway, bus, and tram systems accessible through repairs, renovations, technology, training, and mixed funding.
key_facts: City officials announced the transit accessibility enhancement project on October 15, 2023; it will run over the next three years and covers subway, bus, and tram systems.
A September 20, 2023 report by the local Department of Transportation (DoT) found that more than 30% of subway stations aren't fully accessible.
Barriers listed in the DoT report include non-functioning elevators, escalators often out of service, and transit vehicles misaligned with platforms.
Buses have ramps that are sometimes in disrepair, and some drivers lack proper training on their use.
Immediate fixes include restoring broken elevators, keeping bus ramps operational, and funding emergency maintenance teams that will address breakdowns within 24 hours.
Real-time communication systems, with digital screens and audio announcements, will be added to buses and trains for visually and hearing-impaired passengers.
Long-term renovations include retrofitting older stations with new elevators, redesigning platforms to align with vehicles, and adding tactile guide paths for the visually impaired.
Future stations will have interactive kiosks and wayfinding apps to plot barrier-free routes, locate working elevators, and request assistance via mobile devices.
Public forums and workshops are scheduled for November 2023 so passengers with disabilities and elder citizens can give feedback on the plans.
The estimated $500 million cost is to be covered by municipal bonds, federal grants, and a slight fare increase, according to CFO Laura Schmidt.
The city is seeking private partnerships; companies can receive naming rights for a station or exclusive advertising within the transit networks.
Training for transit staff and drivers will include sensitivity training and operational drills for assisting passengers needing special accommodations.
The DoT committed to regular progress reports and independent accessibility audits conducted annually.
Sidewalks, crosswalks, and public spaces are planned to be addressed in subsequent phases.
